issues.issue: Does the IRPA non-disclosure procedure engage s.7 of the Charter?
issues.applicant_position: Detention and stigma engage his liberty and security of the person interests.
issues.result_quote: it is not necessary to decide whether section 7 of the Charter is engaged. I will assume, without deciding, that it is.

issues.issue: Does judicial review give the affected person an adequate opportunity to challenge non-disclosure?
issues.applicant_position: A single delegate of one Minister lacks political accountability and the expertise and independence to weigh non-disclosure.
issues.result_quote: the Federal Court judge hearing a judicial review involving a confidentiality order made by an Immigration Division member will have an opportunity to review the confidential information

issues.issue: What standard of review applies to a Federal Court judge reviewing an Immigration Division non-disclosure decision?
issues.applicant_position: Review should be deferential, interfering only if the member's decision is patently unreasonable.
issues.result_quote: On balance, I am of the opinion that the proper standard of review on the question of whether relevant information should be disclosed to the affected individual is correctness.

issues.issue: Is the IRPA non-disclosure procedure constitutional under s.7 of the Charter?
issues.applicant_position: The procedure does not accord with fundamental justice and is distinguishable from the former s.40.1 procedure upheld in Ahani.
issues.result_quote: As the IRPA procedure conforms with the principles of fundamental justice, there is no violation of section 7 and the IRPA procedure is constitutional.

issues.issue: Did MacKay J. properly review the Immigration Division's non-disclosure decision?
issues.applicant_position: Did not allege that MacKay J. failed to review properly; the attack was on constitutionality only.
issues.result_quote: This conclusion was open to him and should not be disturbed on appeal.
